title: Ballet Club, writing floor-show arrangements, a week with Benny Carter
summary: He worked about two years at the Ballet Club writing floor-show arrangements for $60, briefly left with Benny Carter, then played with Herbert Leary and Desvigne.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: You remember him? Uptown. And Rico was playing bass. Rico, Alexis? Yeah. Yeah, we called him Rico, you know? Well, we worked there pretty, pretty good while. Oh, about six, eight, no, eleven months I think we worked there. When they sold a place to a guy that called Johnny something, and then, well, he decided to get rid of the band. He didn't want no music there, you know? And then when I left there, then I went to the ballet club. That's on Boynel Street. The ballet club is where the dream room is right now. Oh, now. Yeah, that was the old ballet club. See, Eddie Meloncone had that. Eddie Meloncone had another guy here. Well, I worked there about two years. There about two years. But he used to play all during the war, you know? And he used to have flow shows there. And I used to write all the arrangements for the flow shows. Yeah, all of it. I mean, like if the girl said, well, look, even one thing I want, I just want you to play the chic, play about four chords of the chic, and then the drums would make a break and would do this and would do that. I said, well, look, we don't play that. I said, I got to, we got to have that written on the music, you know? I said, well, all right, well, who could write? I said, well, I'm the fellow who do all the writing for the show. Well, how much are you going to try? I said, $60, you know? And after she didn't got to explain, I remember what she said, you understand? And I just tell the fellows, we'll do the same thing, you understand? Like that, and I get the $60 for nothing. Yeah, that was, yeah, man, I made a lot of money at the back. I used to write for everybody on the show, you know? Yeah, at that time, flow shows, well, they are nothing like what they are now, you know? I mean, what they are now is nothing, you know? But before, these girls were very serious in their work, you know? I mean, they'd go out for all fancy costumes and actually pay money to learn different dances to perform in these clubs, you know? And it was all together different from what's happening now, see? Well, I guess that was around 1943, 44, somewhere along in there, see? Now, let's see, after I left the Ballet Club, where did I go? Yeah, I left the Ballet Club, and this great saxophone player, he also plays trumpet too. Benny Carter. Benny Carter. He came in town. He was looking for a band, for musicians, because the ball was taking all the musicians, you know? So he asked me if I wanted to make a trip with him. So I told him, I said, well, yeah, I said, I'll make a trip. So I think I stayed with Benny about, oh, about a week, you know? And then I came back home, because, matter of fact, I mean, it looked like every night, I mean, you know, every other night somebody would leave the band, you know? And eventually I got to be the only trumpet player, so I just cut out. You know, I just, matter of fact, I didn't even tell him I was gone, you know? I just packed up, you know, one of them nights, and I just left, see? So, well, a union wasn't as strict as that, that time is what they are now, see? So, well, I just cut out. So, then I came back, then I went with, I fooled around New Orleans, I played a different job with Hoevert Leary, Sidney Desveen, who else?
